events.text: A notice goes up on the village gate, in big black characters: a reward in strung cash for every monk caught, by order. The headman reads it out twice. That night someone knocks at your back door, very softly. A monk in a torn grey robe, thin as a rake, straw tied round his sandals. "One bowl of rice a day," he says. "And the attic. Nothing more. I will not be here long."
events.arc: The Thing That Ate the Needle

choices.text: Hide him in the attic, and bring a bowl of rice a day

effects.log: You hide him under the thatch and carry a bowl up the ladder every evening. He eats slowly and spills a few grains every time, and rolls them between his fingers while you talk. A month later your needle is gone from the sewing cushion. In the attic, in the lamplight, a thing the size of a mouse, made of rice grains with a trunk, is chewing on your scissors. The monk looks at it, then at you, and says, "Ah. I am sorry about the needle."

choices.text: Take him to the magistrate

effects.log: You walk him to the magistrate's yard at dawn. He does not struggle. At the gate he turns and says, "Mind your needles," which makes no sense at all. You are paid five taels in strung cash. That night the string in your box is found bitten through, and a few of the coins have toothmarks, and something has walked through the flour.

choices.text: Feed him well, and send him on before dawn

effects.log: You give him rice, soup and a pair of new sandals, and walk him to the edge of the village before the cocks. He bows. On your doorstep in the morning there are three grains of rice pressed into a little shape: four legs, a head, a tail, and something like a trunk. You leave it there. By noon it is gone, and so is the iron latch of your gate.

events.text: Grandmother's needle is gone. The good one, from the silk cushion. Grandmother has turned the house upside down and blamed the cat, the wind and the neighbours. You find it first. Or rather, you find what has it: under the sewing chest, a thing the size of your thumb, made of white cooked rice grains stuck together, with four stubby legs and a tiny trunk. It is chewing the scissors. There is a bright glint of steel inside it, where the needle went.
events.arc: The Thing That Ate the Needle

choices.text: Give it the whole needle-case

effects.log: You push the needle-case under the chest. The little thing sniffs it with its trunk, and then eats the needles one after another, crunch, crunch, like a child eating pine nuts. When it is done it sits back on its rice haunches and looks at you. You could swear it is grateful. Grandmother, finding the empty case, blames the cat again.

choices.text: Sweep it into the kitchen fire

effects.log: You sweep it into the firebox with the broom. A moment later it rolls out again on the other side, unhurt, carrying a burning ember on its back like a bundle of firewood. It holds its little tail high, up and away from the ember, and you notice that: the only part of it that seems afraid. It trots off under the floor. There is a scorch mark on the boards for years.

choices.text: Tell no one, and leave it be

effects.log: You say nothing. Not to Grandmother, not to anyone. Over the next weeks the house loses a spoon, a hairpin, three nails from the gate and the iron ring of the rice chest. You know where they went. When Grandmother finally sees it, at the end of the month, it is the size of a puppy, and she sits down on the floor.

events.text: A death in the house, and the mourning month. You sit up at the mourning table in rough hemp, night after night, with the candle and the rice cakes, because somebody has to. On the fourth night, with nobody left to talk to, you find your fingers pressing a scrap of rice-cake dough into a little beast: four legs, a head, a trunk, a tail. You set it beside the candle. In the morning your hemp-sewing needle is gone, and the dough beast is a little heavier.
events.arc: The Thing That Ate the Needle

choices.text: Keep it, and talk to it at night

effects.log: You keep it. You talk to it every night of the mourning month, about the dead and about yourself, and it listens with its trunk on the table edge. The relatives say the house is haunted because the fire tongs are gone. You say nothing. By the end of the month it follows you about like a dog, and the house has no iron left but the hinges.

choices.text: Give it to a wandering monk who stops at the gate

effects.log: A monk comes begging at the gate on the fifth morning. You put the dough beast in the alms bowl without a word. He looks at it for a long time. "So you made one too," he says, and tucks it into his sleeve, and goes off up the mountain road with a faint crunching sound coming from his robe.

choices.text: Set it on the windowsill and let it go where it likes

effects.log: The relatives want it burned. You set it on the windowsill instead and open the shutter. In the morning it is gone, and so is the iron hook of the shutter. All that spring, in the next village and the next, people find their nails gone and little prints in the dust, and you feel, absurdly, proud.

events.text: Your sword is gone from the rack. So is every lock in the hall, the iron of the well bucket and the cook's best cleaver. A bounty notice has been up in the county town for a month: an ox-sized beast with a hide like a hedge of needles, which cannot be killed. You follow the trail of missing iron up into the hills to an old mine. In the dark, something huge is chewing. Two small eyes, like a rhinoceros's, turn toward your lantern. Your sword is in its mouth, hilt out, like a pipe.
events.arc: The Thing That Ate the Needle

choices.text: Draw qi and duel it for your sword

ok.log: You hit it with everything. Your sword-qi breaks on its needles like water on a rock, and it does not hit back: it does not eat people, you realise, only iron. At last you wrench your sword out of its mouth by the hilt, chewed to the guard. It watches you go, chewing thoughtfully on nothing. You keep the sword, toothmarks and all.

fail.log: Your sword-qi breaks on its needles like water on a rock. It does not fight you. It simply leans on you until you sit down hard in the mud, and then it finishes your sword, crunch, crunch, and goes back to chewing the seam. You walk home bruised and swordless, and laugh about it, years later. (-8 health)

choices.text: Give it the sword, freely

effects.log: You bow and say: take it, then. It is yours. The beast stops chewing. It looks at you a long time, and then it swallows the sword whole, slowly, the way one accepts a gift, and you feel something of your own art go down with it. Years later you will swear you heard your own sword-form spoken in a voice that was not yours.

choices.text: Take the hidden monk's advice: go for its tail with a torch

effects.log: A thin old monk in the next valley told you: everything about it is iron except the tail, and the tail is still rice. You creep round it with a torch. There it is: a pale, grainy tail-tip, like cooked rice. You hold the torch an inch from it. The whole beast goes still, and waits. You lower the torch. You do not know why. It turns its head and looks at you, and you both know you know.

events.text: Your sect sends you to the market town with a purse and an odd errand: "iron-eater needles", which the elders want for a formation. You expect a fraud. Instead a frightened old woman unrolls a cloth on her stall: long grey needles, too long for sewing, faintly warm, with a little rust at the roots as if they had grown. "It sheds them on the hill road," she says, "like a dog sheds hair. Do not tell anyone I sell them."
events.arc: The Thing That Ate the Needle

choices.text: Buy a bundle, as ordered (10 taels)

effects.log: You pay ten taels and carry the bundle home. The elders build their formation with them, and it holds against everything except a summer storm, when the needles all turn, at once, to point north up the hill road. You notice. Nobody else does.

choices.text: Follow her to where she gathers them

effects.log: You follow her at dawn up the hill road. Under a cutting, in the dew, there is a print the size of a cart wheel, and a heap of shed needles, and a long way off something grey and huge going over the ridge. It stops. It looks back at you. Then it goes on, and a little rain of needles falls behind it, like a gift.

choices.text: Buy them all, and carry them back up the hill to it (10 taels)

effects.log: You pay her ten taels for the lot, walk up the hill road and leave the bundle on a flat rock. In the morning the rock is bare, and the bundle's iron clasp is gone too, and there is a ring of tiny dents round the rock where something sat a long time, thinking.

events.text: Every sect under heaven has gathered in the Martial Alliance's great hall for a conclave, and you have a seat on the benches. A hill-sized beast is walking toward the hall. A hundred famous hilts stand out of its needle hide like a hedge: sabres, straight swords, a halberd, things with tassels that once had names. It stops at the steps. When it speaks, it speaks in their old owners' voices, one after another. "I do not take," the voices say. "Not any more. I ask. Will you give me your sword?" Every eye in the hall turns to you.
events.arc: The Thing That Ate the Needle

choices.text: Give it your sword, the first of nine

effects.log: You walk down the steps and hold out your sword, hilt first. The hall is silent. The beast lowers its trunk and takes it as carefully as a child takes a sweet. One new voice joins the others inside it, and it is yours. "One," says the beast. "Thank you." Then it lies down outside the hall and sleeps for three days, and nobody dares wake it.

choices.text: Refuse, and duel the beast that cannot be killed

ok.log: You fight it through the courtyard and across the hill. Nothing you do cuts it. But in the hour when you are nearly spent, you see it, under all that iron: the tail, pale and grainy, like cooked rice. It sees you see. It stops fighting at once and sits down. You walk away with your sword. It lets you.

fail.log: It lets you fight until your arms shake. Nothing cuts it. At last it lies down on top of you, very gently, like a hill deciding to rest, and for a long minute your face is pressed against the one soft thing on it: the tail, which is rice. Then it gets up and walks away and you lie in the grass, knowing. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell it the word its maker left

effects.log: A word comes to you that you were never taught: a silly name, the kind a tired monk would give a thing he made from his own supper. You say it. Every voice in the beast falls silent at once. It puts its trunk to the ground in front of you, like a bow. It does not ask for your sword. It goes away, slowly, and the whole hall breathes out.

choices.text: Walk out of the hall by the back gate

effects.log: You do not give it your sword and you do not fight it. You walk out of the back gate and up the hill and sit down to watch. One by one, the others come out to the beast. Some give, some fight. Late at night it looks up at your hill, a long time, and you have the odd feeling you have been counted anyway.

events.text: Here in the Upper Realm the sword immortals keep a cloud-palace for their conclaves, and you have flown to it on your own blade. Below the cloud steps, the sky is full of something walking. A hill-sized beast is walking toward the hall.
