events.text: Soldiers at the gate at midnight, with torches and a list. Someone has talked. They search the kitchen, the jar terrace, the woodshed. Then the captain looks up at the attic hatch. Its iron ring is gone. Not broken: gone, with little bite marks round the hole. There is no way to pull it open.

choices.text: Shrug: the rats have eaten everything this year

ok.log: "Rats," you say, "eat everything. Look at my sewing cushion." You show them the cushion, picked clean of every needle. The captain laughs, despite himself, and moves on. Up in the thatch, nobody breathes until dawn.

fail.log: The captain does not laugh. He has a soldier poke the hatch with a spear until the thatch rains down. Nothing up there moves. At last they go, and leave you a fine for the trouble you did not cause. The monk comes down at dawn, grey-faced, and thanks you twice.

choices.text: Offer them soup and talk about the harvest

effects.log: You feed six soldiers on what was meant for three days, and talk about the harvest until they yawn. They leave without looking up again. Your family eats thin for a week. In the attic, something chews quietly on the soldiers' forgotten spear-butt cap, which one of them left by the ladder.

events.text: The house has no iron left. The spoons went first, then the chopsticks, then the old brass wedding bowl, then the tobacco pipe. The family eats with wooden spoons now and pretends not to notice. In the rice chest, curled on the rice, a puppy-sized thing of grey needles is asleep, with its pale tail tucked in.

choices.text: Feed it the broken things on purpose

effects.log: You gather every cracked pot, bent nail and broken hoe in the village and feed them to it one at a time. It eats them like a good dog, and leaves the whole spoons alone after that. The monk watches from the ladder. "You are teaching it manners," he says. "Nobody taught me any."

choices.text: Scold it, as you would a dog

effects.log: You scold it. It lowers its trunk and its needles flatten, and it looks so sorry that you have to go outside. That night it eats only the gate hinges, which you suppose is a sort of compromise.

events.text: The monk is leaving. The thing he made is calf-sized now and the attic floor has cracked under it. They go at night, by the back path to the ridge, the monk with his staff and the beast behind him like a big, clinking dog. At the gate the monk stops.

choices.text: Give him the last bowl of rice in the house

effects.log: You give him the last bowl. He eats half and gives the other half to the beast, which eats rice for the first time you have ever seen, very carefully. "So it remembers what it is made of," the monk says. Then they are gone up the ridge, and the house is very quiet and has no iron in it at all.

choices.text: Ask him what he calls it

effects.log: He tells you: a silly name, the kind you give a thing you made from your own supper. You laugh. He laughs too, for the first time in a year. "Do not tell anyone," he says. "Some day it may need someone to say it." You never forget it.

choices.text: Walk them up to the ridge

effects.log: You walk with them to the top of the ridge in the dark. The beast stops at an old mine and sniffs, and its whole hide shivers with joy. The monk sits on a stone. "Here, then," he says. You walk home alone at dawn, and from then on the vein of the mountain rings a little at night.

events.text: You are old. One morning there is a sack on your doorstep, heavy, clinking. Inside: a brass bowl, a tobacco pipe, a dozen spoons, chopsticks, the iron ring of an attic hatch, all a little rusty, all with toothmarks. The old brass wedding bowl is on top.

choices.text: Look up at the ridge, and bow

effects.log: You bow to the ridge. Far off, among the pines, something the size of a hill turns its head. You eat that night with the old brass bowl, and it is the best rice you have tasted in your life.

choices.text: Give the spoons to the families who lost theirs

effects.log: You carry the spoons round the village, house by house. Old people weep over a pipe or a ladle. By evening the sack is empty but for the hatch ring, which you hang over your door.

events.text: The reward money will not stay strung. Every morning the string is bitten through and the coins are fewer, and the ones left have little toothmarks. Your neighbours have started to look at you oddly. Somebody has written "price of a monk" in charcoal on your gate.

choices.text: Give the rest of the money to the temple

effects.log: You carry what is left up to the hill temple and put it in the offering box. The coins clink. Something in the ditch beside the road clinks back. On the way down you feel lighter than you have for a month.

choices.text: Lock it in an iron box

effects.log: You lock the coins in an iron box. In the morning there is no box, and no coins, and in the dust a trail of little prints going toward the magistrate's yard, as if whatever ate it wanted to see where the monk had gone.

events.text: Word comes back from the county town. The monk you handed over was not punished. On the night before his sentence, every lock and chain in the jail was eaten, and the bars, and the jailer's keys. The monk walked out and was never seen again. Something huge was seen going over the ridge.

choices.text: Go and stand outside the empty jail

effects.log: You go and look. The cell door hangs on nothing, its hinges bitten off. You stand there a long time. You are not sure if what you feel is relief or shame. It is both.

choices.text: Laugh, and raise a cup of tea to the monk's health

effects.log: You laugh until you have to sit down, and raise a cup of tea to a monk who must, you think, be a very long way off by now. The tavern looks at you strangely. You do not care.

events.text: Years on, a monk comes begging at your gate, a young one, with a staff too old for him. He looks at you as if he knows your face from a story.

choices.text: Feed him, and ask his pardon for someone else

effects.log: You feed him and tell him, haltingly, what you once did. He listens and nods. "My teacher's teacher told me about a house that sold him," he says. "He said they were frightened, not wicked. He said to eat there if I passed." He eats three bowls.

choices.text: Close the gate

effects.log: You close the gate. Through the crack you watch him walk off down the road with his old staff. That night the iron ring of your gate is gone. Nothing else. Just the ring, as a reminder.

events.text: Some time after the monk passed through, your gate latch is still missing, and the gate swings in the wind. Children say a thing made of rice lives on the ridge and eats the stakes the surveyors drive into the mountain. Tonight, something clinks against your gate.

choices.text: Go out with a lamp

effects.log: At the gate, on the stone, there is a new latch: rough, bent, made of three old nails twisted together, clearly by a trunk and not a hand. It works. You laugh out loud in the dark.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of rice on the step

effects.log: You put out a bowl of rice and go to bed. In the morning the rice is untouched but the bowl's brass rim has been nibbled, delicately, all the way round, like a pie crust. Then a little rice is gone after all. As if it remembered.

events.text: A letter, the first you have ever had from a stranger, carried by a pedlar. It is from the monk. "The thing grows," it says. "It will be very large. If it ever comes to your village, give it something broken. Never something someone needs. It learns from what it is given."

choices.text: Start a heap of broken iron behind the house

effects.log: You start a heap behind the woodshed: cracked pots, bent hoes, rusted nails. Neighbours add to it, laughing. Years later, on a night of a thousand clinks, the heap is gone, and every plough in the village is still there.

choices.text: Keep the letter and tell no one

effects.log: You fold it into your collar and carry it all your life. You never see the thing. But you never quite throw away a broken nail again.

events.text: It came back. Every night now, under the sewing chest, a little clink. It is bigger than a mouse and it has eaten every needle in three houses. Tonight it is sitting in your shoe, waiting, its trunk up.

choices.text: Bring it a bent nail from the gate

effects.log: You bring it a bent nail. It eats it, and climbs into your lap, heavy as a stone, and goes to sleep. You do not move until dawn. Your legs are dead. You have never been happier.

choices.text: Tell it, firmly, no more needles

effects.log: You tell it no more needles. It listens with great seriousness. Next morning the needles are all still there, and the iron ring of the well bucket is gone. You count this as a victory.

events.text: You have been thinking about the ember. The thing rolled out of the fire with a coal on its back and carried it off as if fire were nothing. But it held its tail up and away the whole time. Tonight you find it again, puppy-sized now, nosing at the kitchen fire as if it wanted to eat that too.

choices.text: Pull it back by the scruff

effects.log: You haul it back by the needles of its neck, which is like grabbing a hedgehog made of nails, and it lets you. It looks at the fire and at you. You point at its tail. "Not that," you say. It tucks its tail under, slowly, and you both understand each other.

choices.text: Watch what it does

effects.log: It puts its trunk into the flames and draws in a little fire, like smoke from a pipe, and sneezes, and sits back sulking with its tail curled up high. Not yet, then. You laugh. It sulks more.

events.text: Grandmother knows. She has known for weeks, it turns out. She calls you into the inner room, where the sewing is kept, and points with her pipe at the puppy-sized thing asleep on her silk cushion. "Yours?" she asks.

choices.text: Say yes

effects.log: "Yes," you say. Grandmother sighs. "In my mother's time," she says, "there was a tale of a thing like this. The monks made it. It ate a kingdom." She strokes its needles with one finger. "It does not look like a kingdom-eater. It looks hungry."

choices.text: Say it followed you home

effects.log: "It followed me," you say. Grandmother snorts. "Things like that follow the ones who keep their mouths shut," she says. "Good. Keep it shut." She gives it her bent thimble.

events.text: The thing is too big for the house now. It is the size of a calf, and the floor groans. One night it stands at the gate, looking back at you with its small eyes, and the whole village's iron is clinking inside it.

choices.text: Open the gate for it

effects.log: You open the gate. It goes out into the dark without hurry, and at the corner it stops and lifts its trunk, once, like a wave. You stand in the cold until you cannot hear it any more.

choices.text: Run after it as far as the ridge

effects.log: You follow it to the ridge in your bare feet. At the top it lies down and lets you sit on it, warm iron and needles, and you look at the stars together until you fall asleep. In the morning you are on the grass, under your own coat, and it is gone.

events.text: The relatives have made up their minds. Something in the house eats iron, the fire tongs are gone, the shaman says it is the dead one's restless soul, and the dough beast must be burned at the end of the mourning. They are building the fire in the yard now.

choices.text: Stand between them and the fire

effects.log: You stand in front of the fire in your mourning hemp and say no. A mourner's word carries. The relatives go home grumbling. That night you hear a clink in the dark, and in the morning the tongs are back, a little bent, on the step.

choices.text: Let the shaman look at it

effects.log: The shaman looks for a long time, and puts away her bells, very carefully, where it cannot reach them. "It is not a soul," she says. "It is a beast, and it is grieving with you. Leave it be." The relatives go home. The shaman, on the way out, gives it a broken bell.

events.text: Years later, at the anniversary rite for the one you mourned, you set out the rice cakes as always. At dawn, at the foot of the table, there is a nail. Then another. A little row of nails, set out neat as offerings.

choices.text: Add a nail of your own to the row

effects.log: You add one, a good straight nail. The next year there are two rows. You never see what lays them out. You never need to.

choices.text: Leave a rice cake out beside the nails

effects.log: You leave one rice cake beside the nails. In the morning it is gone, and on the floor, in rice flour, there is the faint print of a foot the size of a soup bowl.

events.text: The bounty on the beast has doubled. Hunters arrive in the county every week, with nets, salt, chains, fire-pots. They have heard you fought it and lived. They want to know how.

choices.text: Tell them the truth: it does not fight back

effects.log: You tell them. Half of them laugh. The other half go home. One old hunter sits with you a long time and then says, "Then what are we hunting it for?" Nobody answers.

choices.text: Sell them a story for supper

effects.log: You tell a fine tale of a battle in the mine, and eat free all month. The hunters go up the ridge and come down with no chains, no nets and no fire-pots. They do not buy you supper after that.

events.text: Your chewed sword hangs on the wall. Visitors ask about the toothmarks. Tonight, cleaning it, you notice the marks are not random: they line up with the weak points of your sword-form, as if the beast had been reading it.

choices.text: Study the marks, and fix the form

effects.log: You spend a winter mending your form where the teeth showed it was weak. In spring you are better than you have ever been. You light incense to a beast, which you never thought you would do.

choices.text: Laugh, and hang it back up

effects.log: You laugh and hang it back. But you keep looking at it.

events.text: Your sect elders are furious. A sword is not a thing you give to a beast. They want you to go back and take it, or be put out of the sect.

choices.text: Say you would give it again

effects.log: You say it. The hall goes silent. You are put to sweeping the courtyard for a year. You sweep it very well. Some evenings you hear the hills clink.

choices.text: Promise to win it back, and do not go

effects.log: You promise, and you do not go. Nobody checks. The elders forget. You never do.

events.text: A traveller passes through and tells a strange tale at the inn: a beast in the south that speaks, in many voices, and one of them recites a sword-form he did not know. He hums the rhythm of it. It is yours.

choices.text: Go and find it

effects.log: You travel a month to a river crossing in the south. It is there, larger than you can believe, and when it sees you it says your sword-form's opening words in your own voice. You sit with it until dark. You do not ask for the sword back.

choices.text: Smile, and let it keep your voice

effects.log: You smile into your cup. Somewhere far off your art goes on being spoken, by something that cannot die. It is not a bad kind of heir.

events.text: Old now, and the young ones ask why you never carried a sword again. You have carried a wooden one for years upon years.

choices.text: Tell them about the beast

effects.log: You tell them. They do not believe you, all but one, who goes to bed thinking about it and dreams of a hedge of hilts. That one, you suspect, will give their sword one day too.

choices.text: Say the wooden one is enough

effects.log: "It is enough," you say, and beat all of them with it, one after another, before lunch.

events.text: A magistrate's man finds you at an inn. The court will pay a fortune to whoever can tell them how to kill the Iron-Eater. Word is, you know. He sets a purse on the table.

choices.text: Say you know nothing

effects.log: "Nothing," you say. He leaves the purse a while, then takes it. You drink your soup. That night you dream of a pale tail in the dark, waiting.

choices.text: Tell him fire, but lie about where

effects.log: You tell him fire, and that the soft place is the eyes. He writes it down. A year later you hear the fire-hunters spent a whole spring burning at its eyes, which only made it glow.

events.text: You meet the beast again by chance on a mountain road. It stops. You both remember the torch. It turns, slowly, and shows you its tail, pale and grainy, as if to say: still here.

choices.text: Put your hand on it, and say: still here

effects.log: You lay your hand on the rice. It is warm. The beast sighs through its trunk like a bellows. When you take your hand away, it goes on up the road, and you go down, and something between you is settled.

choices.text: Bow, and step aside for it

effects.log: You bow and step aside. It goes past you for a long time, it is that big now, and at the end its tail brushes your sleeve, very lightly.

events.text: You have told nobody the secret of the tail in all these years. Tonight someone you trust sits by your fire and asks about the beast.

choices.text: Tell them, and tell them why you never used it

effects.log: You tell them, in a whisper: where the rice is, and that it is the only part of the beast that remembers being made by kind hands. "Do not burn it," you say. "Unless it asks." They nod, white-faced. The secret is kept another lifetime.

choices.text: Keep it to yourself

effects.log: You keep it. Some things should be found, not handed down. You sleep well.

events.text: The needle seller is in trouble. A sect has learned where the iron-eater needles come from and means to set traps on the hill road: iron jaws, baited with ploughshares.

choices.text: Warn the beast: go up the hill road at night

effects.log: You go up at night and sit on the flat rock and talk to the dark about traps. You feel very foolish. In the morning every trap on the road has been eaten, bait and jaws and stakes, neatly, from the outside in.

choices.text: Help the old woman sell faster

effects.log: You help her sell the whole stock in a day and buy her a cart. She leaves the county. The traps catch nothing, and the beast, you hear, stops using that road.

events.text: A shed needle comes to you in the strangest way: it falls out of the sky and sticks in the ground at your feet, quivering, still warm.

choices.text: Keep it as a hairpin

effects.log: You wear it as a hairpin for the rest of your life. On cold nights it is warm. In thunderstorms it hums. Nobody ever tries to steal it twice.

choices.text: Forge it into your sword

effects.log: A smith folds it into your sword. The blade never rusts and never quite stops being hungry: it cuts iron better than anything else. You use that sparingly.

events.text: After the conclave, the Martial Alliance cannot agree on anything. Half the sects call the beast a thief, half call it a judge. They want your word, as the one who faced it.

choices.text: Say it took only what was given

effects.log: You say it. The thief faction walks out. The judge faction asks you to sit at the head of the table. You decline. That night three sect masters come to you privately, each asking how to give a sword without losing face.

choices.text: Say it is neither: it is hungry, and it is learning

effects.log: "Hungry," you say, "and learning manners from us. Mind what we teach it." The hall is quiet a long time. It is quoted for years.

events.text: Years after the conclave, a disciple of a ruined sect comes to you with a broken sword and a question: should they give it to the beast, or bury it with their master?

choices.text: Tell them to give it

effects.log: They give it. The beast takes it gently, and the next day the disciple swears the dead master's voice said goodbye. You do not argue.

choices.text: Tell them to bury it

effects.log: They bury it. Weeks later the grave is undisturbed, and around it, in a ring, are a dozen of the beast's shed needles, set in the earth like a fence.

events.text: The immortals' conclave is in uproar. Since the beast walked the clouds, flying swords refuse to fly south. They turn in their owners' hands and point after it, like needles to a lodestone.

choices.text: Fly south and ask it to let them go

effects.log: You fly south on a sword that pulls like a hound. The beast is lying on a cloud bank, asleep. You ask it, politely. It opens one eye, and sneezes, and every sword in heaven drops back into its owner's hand. You are thanked by four hundred immortals and have no idea what you did.

choices.text: Walk instead

effects.log: You put away your sword and walk the cloud roads for a year. It is slow. It is very beautiful. You find out how much you had stopped looking.

events.text: A child of the Upper Realm, born up here, has never seen iron eaten. They ask you what the beast is for.

choices.text: Say: for stopping

effects.log: "For stopping," you say. "It is learning when to." The child thinks hard. "Are we?" You have no good answer, and you like the child better for it.

choices.text: Take the child to watch it

effects.log: You take the child to the edge of the cloud. Far off, the beast is lying with its trunk on a mountain, chewing an old stake, perfectly content. The child laughs. That is the answer, as it turns out.

events.text: The village wakes to empty hooks. Every kitchen knife is gone, every brass bowl, the hoes from the sheds. Little round prints in the dust go from house to house. The headman calls a meeting.

choices.text: Say it is a beast, not a thief

effects.log: You say you saw it, a puppy-sized thing with a trunk, trotting off with a brass bowl. Half the village laughs. The other half starts locking up their spoons in wooden chests, which, it turns out, works.

choices.text: Organise a watch

effects.log: You organise a watch. On the third night the watchers see it and nobody chases it, because it stops to sniff each of them politely. They come back with sheepish faces and an agreement: leave it the broken things.

events.text: The headman has called a shaman to drive the iron-thief away. She comes with her drum, her fan and her iron bells. By the end of the night's rite, her bells are gone.

choices.text: Help her look for them

effects.log: You help her look. You find one, a single bell, on the threshing floor, bitten in half. She sits down and laughs until she cries. "I have never been answered so plainly," she says.

choices.text: Give her your own little bell

effects.log: You give her the little brass bell you carry for luck. She ties it on. It stays. "Brass," she says. "It does not eat brass, then. Or it does not eat gifts." She looks thoughtful the whole way home.

events.text: Spring, and the village eats with wooden spoons and cooks with clay. The children have started leaving bent nails on the threshing floor at noon, and a calf-sized thing comes and lies down to take them one by one.

choices.text: Bring it a nail yourself

effects.log: You hold out a nail. It takes it from your fingers with its trunk, as gently as a horse takes an apple. Its needles are warm in the sun. The children cheer.

choices.text: Tell the children to stop feeding it

effects.log: You tell them to stop. They look at you as if you were a monster. That evening the beast eats your gate hinges, which seems fair.

events.text: The old widow next door has one plough, and the spring ploughing is in three days. Tonight she is sitting in the field with both arms round its handle, because something calf-sized with a trunk has been circling it all evening.

choices.text: Sit with her all night

effects.log: You sit with her until dawn. The thing comes close twice and both times looks at the two of you and goes away. At sunrise it is lying at the edge of the field, waiting, not for the plough, you think, but to see what you will do.

choices.text: Lend her your plough too, so she has two

effects.log: You carry your own plough over and lay it beside hers. In the morning yours is gone and hers is not. You plough with a borrowed one that spring and grumble, and do not mind as much as you expected.

events.text: A spring without ploughs. The beast has eaten them from every farm in the valley. Farmers turn the soil with sharpened sticks and the earth is hard as a pot. Children go hungry. Nobody dares go near the treeline, where it watches.

choices.text: Go to the treeline and tell it what it did

effects.log: You walk to the trees and tell it, plainly: no ploughs, no rice; no rice, children go hungry. It listens. Then it opens its mouth and coughs, and coughs, and spits a ploughshare out at your feet, then another. Not all of them. But enough for the valley to plant.

choices.text: Dig with a stick beside everyone else

effects.log: You dig with a stick from dawn to dark, beside the others, until your hands bleed. It is the hardest spring of your life. At harvest, the beast is gone from the treeline, and on the threshing floor is a heap of old nails, as if it were paying something back.

events.text: The smith comes up from the market town with a cart of new ploughs, the first in two years. He says a huge beast lay outside his forge all winter, coughing up iron for him to work.

choices.text: Buy the widow a plough first (5 taels)

effects.log: You pay five taels and carry the first plough to the widow. She holds it the way she held the old one, both arms round it, and cries.

choices.text: Ask the smith what it was like

effects.log: "Polite," says the smith. "Very. It coughed up the iron and then waited for me to say thank you."

events.text: You have taken the night watch at the village smithy, because something has been eating the scrap pile and the smith fears for his anvil. On the second night, it comes, calf-sized, and sits down politely beside the scrap, and looks at you.

choices.text: Wave it toward the scrap pile

effects.log: You wave it toward the scrap. It eats the scrap and leaves the anvil, and in the morning the smith is so happy he gives you a knife. The beast, you notice, looks at the knife.

choices.text: Stand in front of the anvil with your spear

ok.log: You stand firm. It sniffs your spear-point, considers, and decides the anvil is not worth the trouble. It eats the scrap and leaves. You did well, you think. It thinks so too, judging by the way it bows its trunk.

fail.log: It eats your spearhead off the shaft, gently, while you are still holding it, and then eats the scrap. The anvil it leaves alone. You go home with a stick. (-2 health)

events.text: The smith has a plan: a bargain with the beast. Scrap every night, as much as the village can gather, in return for leaving the tools alone. You are to be the go-between.

choices.text: Make the bargain, with a handshake to its trunk

effects.log: You shake its trunk. It is cold and very strong. From then on the village scrap pile is empty every morning and the tools are safe. You are the most important person in the village for a whole year.

choices.text: Add a rule: it guards the smithy too

effects.log: You add a clause, feeling silly: it guards the smithy. A month later thieves come for the smith's iron. Nobody ever finds out what happened to them, except that they ran all the way to the next county and their knives were missing.

events.text: A sect recruiter passes through and notices the beast at the smithy. He offers good money to anyone who will help chain it and sell it to his sect as a weapons-eater for their enemies.

choices.text: Refuse him

effects.log: You refuse. He offers more. You refuse again. He leaves angry, and that night his own sword is eaten from its scabbard while he sleeps at the inn.

choices.text: Pretend to agree, then warn it

effects.log: You agree, collect the chains, and feed the chains to the beast that night. The recruiter finds only a smug smith and an empty cart.

events.text: The beast is leaving. It is ox-sized, too big for the village, and the soldiers have heard of it. On its last night it sits by the smithy as always.

choices.text: Give it the smith's old broken anvil, with his blessing

effects.log: The smith brings out his old cracked anvil. The beast eats it slowly, savouring it, and leaves before dawn. The smith keeps the spot by the forge clear for years, as if it might come back.

choices.text: Walk it to the edge of the county

effects.log: You walk it to the boundary stone. It goes on alone. It is the last time you see it, and you think of it whenever you hear a hammer.

events.text: A pedlar in the market is selling "Iron-Eater charms": little iron figures of a beast with a trunk, to hang over the gate so the real one passes you by. They are selling fast.

choices.text: Point out that it eats iron charms first

effects.log: You point out, loudly, that a beast that eats iron will eat iron charms first. The crowd thinks about it. The pedlar packs up fast. That night his cart is found stripped of every nail.

choices.text: Buy one, for the joke (1 tael)

effects.log: You pay one tael and hang it over your gate. In the morning it is gone, and the gate is not. Perhaps it works, in its way.

events.text: An old monk in the market, very thin, sees the charms for sale and laughs until he coughs. "Hang rice," he tells you. "A bowl of rice at the chimney. That it remembers."

choices.text: Ask him how he knows

effects.log: "I knew the one who made it," he says. "We were hiding in the same mountains. He rolled it from his supper. He was lonely." He will say no more, but he shares your lunch.

choices.text: Try it: a bowl at your chimney

effects.log: You put a bowl of rice at the foot of your chimney. Months later, when every house in the street loses its iron, yours keeps its hinges, and the bowl is licked clean.

events.text: The bowl of rice at the chimney is a custom now on your street. Some say it keeps the beast away. Some say it keeps fires away. Some say it keeps away bad dreams.

choices.text: Keep the custom, and say nothing of where it came from

effects.log: You keep the custom. Your grandchildren will keep it without knowing why. That is how customs are.

choices.text: Tell the children the whole story

effects.log: You tell them about the monk and the rice. They decide the bowl is for the beast's tail, so it does not forget. Children are often right.

events.text: A bounty hunter hires you as a second hand. She has a sack of salt, a whip and a torch, and an old book that says these are what drive the Iron-Eater off. "Not kill," she says. "Nobody kills it. Drive it off, collect the county's money."

choices.text: Go with her

effects.log: You go. You carry the salt. The tracks lead to an old mine, and you camp outside it, and in the night you hear it chewing the seam, contented as an ox.

choices.text: Ask why salt

effects.log: "Salt rusts iron," she says. "A whip is leather; it cannot eat it. Fire makes it glow, and a glowing thing is easy to follow." She has thought about this a long time. You go with her.

events.text: In the mine mouth, at dawn. The beast is ox-sized, sleeping across the gallery, needles rising and falling. The hunter hands you the salt. "Throw it in its face," she whispers.

choices.text: Throw the salt

ok.log: The salt hits it in the face. It sneezes like a forge and backs into the dark, offended. The hunter collects the county's money and gives you half. You feel oddly ashamed.

fail.log: The salt hits it in the face. It sneezes and the blast knocks you both flat. It walks over you very carefully, without treading on anyone, and out into the morning. (-4 health)

choices.text: Put the salt down and wake it gently

effects.log: You put down the salt and say, out loud, good morning. It opens its eyes and looks at you both. The hunter freezes. Then it gets up and walks out of the mine, as if it had been meaning to leave anyway. The county pays all the same.

events.text: Round the campfire, the hunter tells you why she hunts it. Her family's village was the first to lose its ploughs, years ago, and the first to go hungry.

choices.text: Say it can be made to give them back

effects.log: You tell her about the smiths who say it coughs up iron when asked. She stares into the fire. "Asked," she says. "Nobody ever asked." In the morning she has gone toward the mine, without the salt.

choices.text: Listen, and say nothing

effects.log: You listen. Some stories only need someone to hear them. She sleeps better that night than you have seen her sleep.

events.text: Years later a letter from the hunter. Her village has ploughs again: the beast lay in the field all one spring and spat them out, one a day. She has hung up the whip.

choices.text: Visit her village at harvest

effects.log: You visit at harvest. The fields are gold. In the village square there is a rusted mound with nails left on it for luck. The hunter, grey now, laughs to see you.

choices.text: Write back, and hang up a weapon of your own

effects.log: You write back and hang up one of your own weapons, the one you liked least. It feels like a beginning of something.

events.text: Your sect's treasured blade, handed down for nine generations, has been eaten. The beast took it from the shrine in one bite. The sect master wants to go after it with every disciple. You are to lead the way.

choices.text: Lead them, but make them leave their swords behind

effects.log: You make them leave their swords. They grumble. At the ravine the beast watches a hundred unarmed disciples come and looks, if anything, impressed.

choices.text: Lead them, armed

effects.log: You lead them armed. By the end of the day the beast has eaten forty swords and is lying down, very full. Nobody is hurt but the sect's pride.

events.text: The sect master stands before the beast and asks for the blade back. It does not move. Then, from inside it, a voice speaks: the sect's founder, dead nine generations, scolding the master for his posture.

choices.text: Ask the founder's voice what it wants

effects.log: "Want?" says the founder's voice. "I want this one to stand properly." The master stands properly. The beast coughs up the blade at his feet, and turns, and goes. The master weeps all the way home.

choices.text: Draw and challenge it for the blade

ok.log: You fight it until dusk. Your sword-qi does nothing. But at the end it coughs up the blade, as if you had made your point. The master never asks how.

fail.log: It eats your sword too. Then, as if sorry, it coughs up the sect's blade at the master's feet and leaves with yours. (-6 health)

events.text: The blade is back on its stand, toothmarks on the guard. The sect master cannot stop looking at it. "It gave it back," he keeps saying. "Why would it give it back?"

choices.text: Say: so you could give it freely

effects.log: You say it. The master is silent for a month. Then, one morning, he takes the blade off its stand and walks out of the gate with it, toward the hills. He comes back empty-handed and looking ten years younger.

choices.text: Say: it did not like the taste

effects.log: The master laughs for the first time since spring. You are promoted. The blade stays on its stand and the sect stays proud, and you wonder, now and then, what the other answer would have been.

events.text: A letter, years later, from a sect far away: their master gave the beast a sword, and a sword came back with it, a blade with toothmarks on the guard that the beast once took from your sect.

choices.text: Go and see it

effects.log: You go and see it. It is your sect's old blade, without doubt, given on and on, master to beast to master. You hold it, and give it back, and go home lighter.

choices.text: Laugh, and let it travel

effects.log: You laugh. A sword that goes from hand to hand by gift is a better heirloom than one on a stand.

events.text: The court has hired the best to end the beast, and you are the best. The plan is fire: fire-pots, burning straw, a ravine of dry brush. "Only fire can kill it," says the court's man. "Find the soft place."

choices.text: Take the commission

effects.log: You take it. The money is very good and the beast, everyone says, has eaten three villages' ploughs. You walk the hills for a month, learning its habits.

choices.text: Take it, and plan to fail

effects.log: You take it, smiling, and resolve to do it badly. The court's man looks at you a long time. He is not stupid.

events.text: You have watched it for a month. You know now. Everything is iron except the tail-tip, pale and grainy as cooked rice, and it keeps that tucked away from fire always.

choices.text: Keep the secret from the court

effects.log: You report: no soft place. The court's man writes it down and looks at you hard. The fire-hunt goes ahead and burns the ravine and the beast walks out of the flames red-hot and unhurt, carrying them into a village. Nobody dies. Three barns burn. You carry the guilt of it a long time.

choices.text: Go and warn the beast

effects.log: You climb to its ridge at night and tell it about the ravine. It looks at you for a long time. The next day it is gone from the province, and the court's man finds the ravine full of dry brush and no beast.

events.text: The court's man finds you. He knows you knew. "Tell me where the rice is," he says, "or the court will know whose side you are on."

choices.text: Tell him nothing

effects.log: You tell him nothing. You lose the court's favour and your fee. The beast lives. When you think about it, which is often, you find you would do it again.

choices.text: Fight your way out

ok.log: You leave him on the floor of the inn and are three provinces away by morning. He does not follow. You are a fugitive for a year and the beast is never told.

fail.log: He is better than you thought. You get away bruised and three provinces away before you can breathe. (-8 health)

events.text: Years on, the beast passes your house in the night. You hear it stop. In the morning, on your step, there is a torch, old and charred, the kind the court's fire-hunters carried, bitten neatly in half.

choices.text: Hang it over the door

effects.log: You hang the two halves over your door, crossed. Nobody else knows what they mean. You do.

choices.text: Burn it in your stove

effects.log: You burn it in your stove. It is only a torch, after all. But the stove draws better than it ever has, all that winter.

events.text: The one who taught you everything is some years dead. Their sword was lost in the war. Tonight, on the road, a voice calls your name from the dark: their voice. Out of the dark comes an elephant-sized beast with a hedge of hilts, and one of them is the sword you lost.

choices.text: Answer the voice

effects.log: You answer. The voice speaks, from inside the beast: your teacher's old corrections, the way they always said them, impatient and kind. You sit in the road and listen until dawn. Then the beast goes, and you are able, for the first time since, to weep.

choices.text: Demand the sword back

effects.log: You demand it. The beast is quiet. Then the voice, your teacher's, says, "Leave it. It is learning from me." You stand in the road for a long time.

events.text: The beast comes back to your road, again and again. Each time your teacher's voice gives you a lesson you never had in life: the one they meant to teach you before the war.

choices.text: Learn it

effects.log: You learn it. It takes years of nights on the road. At the end of it, you understand something about your art that no one living knows.

choices.text: Ask the voice whether it is really them

effects.log: "No," says the voice. "I am what was left in the steel. But what was left was true." That is enough.

events.text: Another student of the same teacher has heard of the voice, and wants to use it: to ask where their teacher's hidden manuals were buried.

choices.text: Bring them to it, and let the voice decide

effects.log: You bring them. The voice listens and says, "Under the plum tree. Share them." The other student weeps and agrees. The manuals are dug up and copied for all who want them.

choices.text: Refuse: the dead should not be mined

effects.log: You refuse. The other student curses you. Years later, you are told the voice gave the manuals' place to a stranger child who asked kindly. You find you do not mind.

events.text: The last night the beast comes. Your teacher's voice says goodbye, plainly, and adds that you are better than they ever were.

choices.text: Say thank you

effects.log: You say thank you. The beast lowers its trunk and goes. You never hear the voice again. You hear it in yourself, which is better.

choices.text: Give the beast your own sword, so the voice has company

effects.log: You give it your sword. Two voices now, teacher and student, travelling together in the iron. You hope they argue.

events.text: A general from the north-east, ambitious and clever, sends for you. An invading army is camped at the river. He has heard you can find the Iron-Eater. "Bring it to their camp," he says, "and let it eat their weapons in a night. Nobody dies, and the war is over."

choices.text: Agree to ask it

effects.log: You agree to ask it, not command it. The general nods: he knows the difference. You go up into the hills.

choices.text: Ask what he will do with the war, afterwards

effects.log: You ask. He is quiet, then honest: "Take the throne, one day." You consider him a long time and go up into the hills anyway, because a war ended without blood is still a war ended.

events.text: The beast lies in a high valley, elephant-sized, chewing ore. You explain the war, the army, the general. It listens, its trunk on the ground.

choices.text: Ask it plainly

effects.log: You ask. It gets up. That night, at the river, the invaders' camp wakes to find no spears, no swords, no arrowheads, no cooking pots. By noon they are walking home. The general is very pleased. The beast is very full.

choices.text: Tell it to choose for itself

effects.log: You tell it the whole thing, both sides, and leave the choice to it. It goes down to the river at dusk and eats both armies' weapons, impartially, and lies down between them. There is no war. There is a great deal of shouting.

events.text: Years later the general is a great man. He sends for you again: he wants the beast to eat the weapons of the old court's last loyal general, a stubborn old man who regards gold as nothing but stones.

choices.text: Refuse him

effects.log: You refuse. The general's face does not change, but you are not invited to court again. The old loyal general dies anyway, in his own time and by other hands, and you learn later that the beast was at the execution ground, and took his sword, given, from his hand.

choices.text: Carry the message to the beast, and let it answer

effects.log: You carry it. The beast listens and does not go. Instead it goes to the old general's house and waits outside the gate, and when the old general comes out, he unbuckles his sword and gives it, freely. The beast walks away with it. The ambitious general never asks you again.

events.text: A new dynasty. The kingdom you were born in is gone. People in the old capital have a saying now, for any trouble nobody can stop: "like the Iron-Eater of Songdo's last days."

choices.text: Correct them

effects.log: You tell them it stopped a war, once. They look at you as if you were very old, which you are.

choices.text: Use the saying yourself

effects.log: You find yourself using the saying. It is apt. You laugh at yourself, quietly.

events.text: Your sect and its rival have warred for three generations over one sword: a famous blade each side says is theirs. The elders have run out of ideas, and they send you down with the sword. The beast is lying in the gorge between the two sects, waiting, as if it knew.
events.arc: A Sword to End a War

choices.text: Give it the sword

effects.log: You walk down to the gorge with the sword and give it. The rival leader, watching from the far bank, is silent a long time. Then they walk down too and bow to you. Three generations of war end in an afternoon because there is nothing left to fight over.

choices.text: Offer the rival half the sword's honour

effects.log: You carry the rival a letter offering joint keeping. It takes years of meetings. In the end you both give the sword to the beast together, standing side by side.

events.text: The young of both sects grumble: the old ones gave away the thing they were supposed to inherit. Some want to fight the beast for it.
events.arc: A Sword to End a War

choices.text: Let them try

ok.log: You go with them. The beast plays with them all day like a big dog with pups and gives nothing back. By sunset they are laughing. That is what you wanted.

fail.log: They fail, and so do you, with them, and you all lie in the grass bruised and laughing at the sky. (-6 health)

choices.text: Teach them the art the sword was famous for, with wooden swords

effects.log: You teach the art with wooden swords. It turns out the art was never in the steel. The young of both sects learn it together.

events.text: Long years of peace between the two sects. A child of the rival sect marries into yours. At the wedding, far off on the hill, the beast lifts its trunk.
events.arc: A Sword to End a War

choices.text: Raise a cup to it

effects.log: You raise a cup to the hill. Everyone turns to look. The old ones of both sects raise theirs too.

choices.text: Send it the wedding's old cooking pots

effects.log: You send it the old cracked cooking pots from the feast. It eats them that night with every sign of enjoyment.

events.text: The palace is burning. The court has sent for you: you are the one the beast is known to listen to. "Lead it in," says a minister, white with soot. "They say it eats fire. If it does not, we lose the hall and the records."

choices.text: Walk into the courtyard beside it

effects.log: You walk into the heat beside the beast. At the steps of the burning hall it lowers its trunk and begins to drink the fire, as if it were a river, and grows red, then white, and the flames go into it, room by room. By dawn the hall stands, black and smoking and whole.

choices.text: Ask it, first, whether it wants to

effects.log: You ask it. It looks at the fire a long time, and then at the minister, and then at you. Then it goes in. It wanted to be asked. Most of the hall is saved.

events.text: After the fire, the court is afraid of what it saw. A beast that eats fire cannot be killed by anything. Some ministers want it driven out of the kingdom. They want you to do it.

choices.text: Refuse, in front of the whole court

effects.log: You refuse in open court. There is an uproar. The king, quiet at the back, says only: "It saved the records of five hundred years." The matter is dropped.

choices.text: Go and talk to it about where it might live

effects.log: You go and talk to it. It decides, after a week, on an old mine in the hills behind the palace, near enough to come if called. The court calls this a victory. So does it.

events.text: A mason in the palace works on a new chimney behind the queen's hall: hexagonal, orange brick, longevity motifs. At the foot of it he is carving a bear-like beast with a trunk.

choices.text: Tell him what it really looks like

effects.log: You tell him: the needles, the small eyes, the rice-pale tail. He carves it truer than any picture. People who see it say it looks as if it might get up.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of rice at the foot of it

effects.log: You leave a bowl of rice at the foot of the chimney. The mason does not laugh. He leaves a bowl too, the next day.

events.text: The palace burns again, many years on, in a war. This time nobody sends for anyone. You go anyway.

choices.text: Go to the hills and call it

effects.log: You go to the hills and call for it, loudly, the way you would call a dog. It wakes, looks at the glow in the sky, and goes. You follow and watch it eat a war's fire.

choices.text: Fight the fire with the buckets, beside the servants

effects.log: You fight it with buckets all night beside the servants. Near dawn, a vast red shape comes over the hill and finishes it. You are too tired to be surprised.

events.text: You are set to guard the queen's hall. The queen has not slept in a month for nightmares. Tonight a grey beast, huge and quiet, comes over the palace wall and lies down at the foot of her chimney.

choices.text: Stand guard, and let it be

effects.log: You let it be. Through the night you watch dark shapes like smoke drift out of the queen's window and into its trunk. At dawn the queen wakes rested for the first time in a month. The beast is gone.

choices.text: Challenge it on the steps

ok.log: You draw. It does not rise. It only looks at you, and you understand that it is working, and that you are interrupting. You put your sword away, embarrassed.

fail.log: You strike, and your sword sinks into its hide like a spoon into porridge and is gone. It does not even turn its head. (-5 health)

events.text: The court wants to know what came over the wall. The queen, rested, says she dreamed of a beast eating her bad dreams like rice cakes. The ministers want to hunt it.

choices.text: Tell them what you saw

effects.log: You tell them. The queen orders it left alone. She orders rice left at the foot of her chimney every night. It is done for generations.

choices.text: Say you saw nothing

effects.log: You say nothing. The ministers hunt and find nothing. The beast comes back every night that month, and you stand guard, and nobody thanks either of you.

events.text: A bad dream of your own: the old war, every face. You wake in a sweat in the guardhouse. Outside the door, grey in the moonlight, the beast is lying with its trunk at the crack.

choices.text: Open the door and let it in

effects.log: You open the door. It does not come in. It just breathes in, once, and the dream goes into it like smoke, and you sleep till noon, the best sleep of a hundred years.

choices.text: Keep the dream

effects.log: You tell it, through the door: no. That one is mine. It waits a moment, and then goes. You lie awake. It is your dream. You keep it.

events.text: The queen is old, and dying. She asks for you. "The beast," she says, "I would like to thank it. Will it come?"

choices.text: Go and bring it

effects.log: You go to the hills and ask. It comes. It lies at the foot of her chimney all her last night, and she dies in her sleep, without a dream at all.

choices.text: Say it is already here

effects.log: You go to the window. It is already there, at the foot of the chimney, grey and patient. She smiles.

events.text: Word goes round the murim: the beast has been given eight famous swords, freely, by eight masters. A ninth, it is said, and it will become something else. You are asked to witness.

choices.text: Go and witness

effects.log: You go. On the mountain path at dawn the ninth master, old and frightened, walks down to it with the sword held out. You watch the sword go into the beast and something in the whole mountain change, like a breath let out.

choices.text: Offer to be the ninth yourself

effects.log: You offer. The masters look at you oddly: it is not yours to offer, they say, it is already decided. But the beast, when it passes you, stops and looks, as if it had heard.

events.text: Since the ninth sword, no blade in the murim has been raised against the beast. Sects train with wooden swords. Some masters say the murim is finished.

choices.text: Say it is beginning

effects.log: "It is beginning," you say, and take up a wooden sword, and teach. Your students are the best in a generation.

choices.text: Keep your steel sword, for now

effects.log: You keep your steel. Somebody should remember how. But you never draw it again.

events.text: A human at your level, an old rival, comes to you with a strange plan: to walk up the mountain to the beast and ask to stop with it. To end their life as it ends its own: by choosing.

choices.text: Walk with them

effects.log: You walk up the mountain with your old rival. The beast listens, and lies down, and your rival lies down beside it in the sun. You come down alone. You understand, better than before, what a life is for.

choices.text: Talk them out of it

effects.log: You talk all night. In the morning they laugh and say they only wanted to hear you argue for them. You both go and visit the beast anyway, and come back down together.

events.text: Your flying sword was eaten out of the sky on your way to court. You land on a cloud bank, swordless and furious, beside a beast the size of a hill, chewing. Heaven's armoury, you remember, is only a day's walk from here.

choices.text: Demand your sword back

effects.log: You demand it. It coughs it up, bent, chewed, and slick with something like rust. Then it looks, pointedly, toward heaven's armoury. You understand that it is asking. You fly off on a bent sword to warn the keepers.

choices.text: Sit down beside it and ask why

effects.log: You sit and ask. It answers in the voice of a sword immortal dead ten thousand years: heaven has more swords than it needs. You find it hard to argue.

events.text: The keepers of heaven's armoury want the beast stopped before it reaches the gates. They want an immortal who has met it to stand at the gate with them.

choices.text: Stand at the gate, and let it ask

effects.log: You stand at the gate. It comes, and asks. The keepers, after a long argument, give it the swords no one has drawn in ten thousand years. It eats them slowly. Heaven feels lighter.

choices.text: Stand at the gate, sword raised

ok.log: It stops at your sword-point, considers you, and goes away. The keepers cheer. You feel, somehow, that you won the wrong argument.

fail.log: It eats your sword and walks round you and sits down at the gate, and waits to be asked properly. In the end the keepers ask it in. (-8 health)

events.text: An immortal envoy is sent to ask the beast what it will eat next. Heaven wants a list. You are the envoy.

choices.text: Ask

effects.log: You ask. It thinks a long time and says, in a dozen voices: "Whatever is given." Heaven is not satisfied. You are.

choices.text: Do not ask; bring it a gift instead

effects.log: You bring it an old cracked incense burner from your own hall. It eats it, delighted. You report to heaven: what it will eat next is up to us.

events.text: Heaven sends you down to persuade the beast to stop. It has been eating for ages. Nobody can make it stop. They hope, they say, it might choose to.

choices.text: Ask it what it would be, if it stopped

effects.log: You ask. It is quiet a long time. Then it says, in the voice of a hungry monk you never met: "A bell. A plough. A chimney. Rice." You write them all down.

choices.text: Tell it heaven is afraid

effects.log: You tell it the truth: heaven is afraid of it. It seems surprised. It seems, almost, sorry.

events.text: A heavenly immortal joins you on your errand. They tell you, quietly, that long ago, when they were a mortal child, they fed this beast nails on a threshing floor.

choices.text: Bring them to it

effects.log: You bring them. The beast knows them at once, somehow, and lies down and lets them climb on its trunk the way they did when they were small. Neither of you mentions stopping again that year.

choices.text: Ask what the beast was like then

effects.log: "Hungry," they say. "And kind about it. It never took the nail until you held it out."

events.text: Your report to heaven is due. The beast has not stopped. It has, however, stopped taking. It eats only what is given.

choices.text: Report: it has stopped, in the way that matters

effects.log: You report it so. Heaven argues for an age and accepts it.

choices.text: Report: it will stop when it is ready, and not before

effects.log: You report it plainly. Heaven is annoyed. The beast, when you tell it, laughs in nine voices.

events.text: The beast comes to your throne in the heavens and asks, in a hundred voices, for the last sword in the heavens: yours, forged before the world.
events.arc: The Last Sword in the Heavens

choices.text: Give it

effects.log: You give it. There is no sword left in heaven. For a moment everyone is afraid. Then they start learning to live without one.

choices.text: Ask it why

effects.log: "So that nobody ever has to draw it," the voices say. You think about that for a year, and then you give it.

choices.text: Refuse

effects.log: You refuse. It bows and goes away and does not ask again. You keep the sword, and never draw it, and in the end, it is the same.

events.text: A sovereign of a rival heaven sends an envoy: will you help turn the beast loose on their armoury?
events.arc: The Last Sword in the Heavens

choices.text: Say no, and send the envoy home with a wooden sword

effects.log: You send the envoy home with a wooden sword. The rival heaven, puzzled, keeps it. A century later they send one back.

choices.text: Say it does not take, it asks

effects.log: "It asks," you say. "Ask your own armoury whether it would like to be asked." The envoy goes home thoughtful.

events.text: A quiet evening at the edge of heaven. The beast lies with its trunk across your threshold. You are both very old.
events.arc: The Last Sword in the Heavens

choices.text: Sit with it

effects.log: You sit with it until the stars come out. Neither of you says anything. It is the best evening in ten thousand years.

choices.text: Ask it what it misses

effects.log: "Rice," it says, in one voice only, a voice you have never heard: its own.

events.text: A storyteller in the teahouse tells the tale of the beast of Songdo's last days, which ate every needle in the capital and could not be killed. "Eating like the Iron-Eater eats iron," he finishes, and the room laughs, and looks at the fattest man there.

choices.text: Ask how the story ends

effects.log: "It depends who tells it," he says. "Some say fire at the tail. Some say a monk's staff. Some say it still lives." He winks. "I say it still lives."

choices.text: Buy the storyteller a cup

effects.log: You buy him a cup and he tells you the parts he leaves out for the crowd: the rice, the attic, the lonely monk. You go home with your head full.

events.text: You catch yourself using the proverb: someone has caused trouble no one can stop, and you call them a Songdo's last-days Iron-Eater. A child asks what that means.

choices.text: Tell the child the whole tale

effects.log: You tell it, all of it. The child's favourite part is the rice tail. Children always like that part.

choices.text: Say it means someone who does not know when to stop

effects.log: "Someone who does not know when to stop," you say. The child thinks. "Did it ever learn?" You do not know.

events.text: A magistrate with a bad reputation is eating the county alive: taxes, fines, a new levy every month. In the market people mutter the proverb about him. Then one night every lock, chain and cash box in his office is eaten, and the tax ledgers are found lying in the square, open, held down by nothing.

choices.text: Read the ledgers out loud to the market

effects.log: You read them out, page by page, to a crowd that grows all morning. By noon the county knows exactly what it was charged and what it owed. The magistrate leaves before dusk. Nobody uses the proverb about him again; they use it about the beast, and fondly.

choices.text: Look for tracks

effects.log: You look for tracks. There are none. Just a faint smell of rust, and, on the doorstep of the office, three grains of rice pressed together into a shape. You leave them there.

events.text: Surveyors have been driving iron stakes into the ridge above your village, to cut the mountain's veins, people say. Every morning the stakes are gone. Holes, and little toothmarks in the earth.

choices.text: Leave a stake out yourself, at the mine mouth

effects.log: You leave one at the mine mouth, a rusty one. In the morning it is gone and a single shed needle lies in its place, as long as your forearm.

choices.text: Warn the surveyors off

effects.log: You tell the surveyors the ridge eats stakes. They laugh. After a month of vanishing stakes they stop laughing and go away.

events.text: Since the stakes stopped, the ridge has been green and the spring above the village runs clearer. Old people say the mountain was in pain and something ate the pain.

choices.text: Go up and say thank you at the mine

effects.log: You go up and say it. From deep in the mine comes a long, contented crunch, like an old man eating a radish.

choices.text: Plant a pine where the last stake was

effects.log: You plant a pine. It grows very straight.

events.text: A rockfall closes the old mine mouth above the village. From inside, all night, comes a sound like a mountain chewing its way out, very slowly, and in no hurry at all.

choices.text: Dig from the outside to meet it

effects.log: You dig from the outside with three neighbours. At dawn the last stone falls inward, and in the dark beyond it two small eyes blink at your lantern, and something sneezes rock dust over all of you.

choices.text: Leave it be: it is in no hurry

effects.log: You leave it. A month later the mine mouth is open again, neater than before, and a heap of chewed stone lies outside it like the spoil of a very careful miner.

events.text: Your house's chimney has a little beast carved at its foot: a bear with a trunk. Your family has always left a bowl of rice there on the last night of the year. This year it is your turn.

choices.text: Leave the bowl, and say the old words

effects.log: You leave the bowl and say the words: eat the sparks, eat the bad dreams. That year nobody in the house has a nightmare, and the kitchen fire never once spits.

choices.text: Leave the bowl, and add a nail

effects.log: You add a nail, on impulse. In the morning the rice is untouched and the nail is gone, which makes the old woman of the house laugh for a whole day.

events.text: A fire in the street. Sparks rain on every roof. Yours, the only one with a carved beast at the chimney's foot, does not catch.

choices.text: Carry water to the neighbours

effects.log: You carry water all night. In the morning neighbours ask you how. You show them the carving, and the bowl. By next year there are carvings at the foot of a dozen chimneys.

choices.text: Kneel and thank the carving

effects.log: You kneel and thank it. The brick is warm, very warm, as if something had eaten a great many sparks.

events.text: The sects train with wooden swords now. Every one of them. The old ones say there was a time when blades were steel and people died of them, and you think they are making it up. Today the old village teacher takes the children to the valley where the great sleeping beast lies, with a hundred hilts on its back, and you go along.

choices.text: Climb it, like the other children

effects.log: You climb it. The hilts are warm. From the top you can see the sea. You understand, sitting there, why nobody makes steel swords any more: there is nothing left that anyone wants to fight for.

choices.text: Ask the teacher what the hilts are

effects.log: "Gifts," the teacher says. "Every one of them given. None taken. That is why nobody raises a blade any more." You look at it a long time.

events.text: A bandit with a real steel sword comes to your village. Nobody has seen one in years. He waves it about. Nobody is afraid of it, which seems to confuse him enormously.

choices.text: Disarm him with your wooden sword

effects.log: You disarm him with your wooden sword in three moves. He sits down in the road, astonished. You take him to the valley and he gives the sword to the beast, and cries, and joins the village.

choices.text: Ask him who he is going to fight with it

effects.log: "Everyone," he says. "Who?" you say. He looks round the village: farmers, children, old people with wooden swords. He puts it down.

events.text: There is a field near your village where the ploughs turn up old iron every spring: needles, spoons, a brass bowl, sword hilts, all with toothmarks. People say a beast once let someone burn its tail, and everything it had ever eaten poured out and went home. This spring, a neighbour's plough turns up a spoon with your family's mark on it, and it is brought to you.

choices.text: Take it home to the family altar

effects.log: You carry it home and set it on the family altar. The old woman of the house looks at it and goes very quiet. "Your great-great-grandmother's," she says. "It came home."

choices.text: Leave it in the field for its owners

effects.log: You leave it. Some things want to find their own way. The next week it is gone from the field, and a family three villages off has a wedding spoon back.

events.text: You find a sword in the field of iron, half rusted, a famous blade by the look of the guard. A sect would pay a fortune for it.

choices.text: Take it to the sect it came from

effects.log: You carry it to the sect. The elders weep. They offer you money; you refuse. They name a hall after you instead, which is more embarrassing.

choices.text: Bury it again

effects.log: You bury it again in the field of iron. It is not yours. You go home with an odd feeling of having done something correctly.

events.text: You serve in the palace. Behind the queen's hall there is a chimney with a carved beast at its foot, and a rule older than anyone: a bowl of rice there every night. Tonight the bowl is yours to carry.
events.arc: The Beast at the Chimney's Foot

choices.text: Carry it, and say good night to the beast

effects.log: You set down the bowl and say good night, feeling silly. The brick under your hand is warm. That night nobody in the palace dreams badly.

choices.text: Ask the old guard why

effects.log: "It eats the sparks coming up and the bad dreams coming down," the old guard says. "For ever. Least we can do is feed it."

events.text: A fire breaks out in the queen's kitchen. Sparks pour up the chimney. You run to the courtyard and stop: the sparks are going down, into the carved beast's trunk, and out of sight.
events.arc: The Beast at the Chimney's Foot

choices.text: Bow to it

effects.log: You bow. Nobody else saw. You never tell anyone, but every night after that you carry the bowl yourself.

choices.text: Bring the rice early, and two bowls

effects.log: You bring two bowls that night. In the morning both are licked clean, and the brick is warm as a hearth.

events.text: The great bell at the capital's crossroads rings the gates open at dawn and shut at dusk. Everyone knows it rings slightly flat. You have been made a bell-ringer's apprentice.

choices.text: Ring it as it is

effects.log: You ring it. The note goes out across the city, slightly flat, and the gates open, and you feel it in your teeth like something alive.

choices.text: Ask why it rings flat

effects.log: "It was cast from a beast," the old ringer says, "that lay down in the founders' pit of its own will. Something in it was never quite iron."

events.text: On a quiet night you are alone in the bell pavilion, and you put your hand on the bronze. It is warm, and very faintly, from deep inside, something is chewing.

choices.text: Whisper good night to it

effects.log: You whisper good night. The chewing stops, and the bell gives a tiny hum, like a contented sigh.

choices.text: Bring it an old nail

effects.log: You bring it a nail and lay it in the bell's mouth. In the morning the nail is gone. The bell rings a little less flat that dawn.

events.text: In your village temple there is an old wooden staff, kept behind the altar, which the monks say once stopped a beast that could not be killed. You are asked to clean it.

choices.text: Clean it carefully

effects.log: You clean it. It is just wood, worn smooth by a hand. But your fingers fit the worn place, exactly, as if they had held it before.

choices.text: Ask the monks the story

effects.log: "The beast asked to be struck," the old monk says. "Once. It spat out everything it had eaten, and was gone. That was the kindest thing anyone ever did for it, and the hardest."

events.text: A smith comes to the temple: in his forge there is a great heap of old iron, which, he swears, came out of the beast the day the staff struck it. He wants the temple to bless it.

choices.text: Bless it with the staff

effects.log: You touch the heap with the staff. Nothing happens. Then all the iron, at once, gives a faint ring, like a bell a long way off.

choices.text: Tell him to make ploughs of it

effects.log: You tell him to make ploughs. He does. Every one of them is lucky.

events.text: Every plough in your valley was once the same beast, the old people say: it lay down in a famine year and let the smiths melt it into ploughs. Yours is old and good. This spring it hums as it turns the earth.

choices.text: Plough on, humming with it

effects.log: You hum along. The furrows come out straight as a ruler. The harvest is the best in years.

choices.text: Stop and listen

effects.log: You stop and listen. It is not a hum. It is something very old, chewing contentedly on the earth.

events.text: A famine in the next valley. Their ploughs were lost in a flood. Your valley has spare ones, old ones.

choices.text: Carry ploughs over the pass

effects.log: You carry six ploughs over the pass on your back. That autumn the next valley eats.

choices.text: Persuade the village to give half

effects.log: It takes three meetings. In the end the village gives half its ploughs. Nobody goes hungry on either side of the pass.

events.text: In the old mine above your village lives something small, grey and needle-haired with a trunk. It eats the vein-cutters' stakes by morning and the province says it is the happiest creature in the world.
events.arc: The Happiest Creature in the Province

choices.text: Bring it a rusty stake

effects.log: You bring it a stake. It eats it like barley sugar and lies on its back in the sun. You laugh until you cry.

choices.text: Sit at the mine mouth and watch

effects.log: You sit all day. It does nothing at all but gnaw the mountain and doze. You go home rested in a way you cannot explain.

events.text: Surveyors come to cut the mountain's vein with iron stakes, by order. By morning every stake is gone, and the surveyors' iron cooking pot too.
events.arc: The Happiest Creature in the Province

choices.text: Feed the surveyors

effects.log: You feed them at your house. They give up after a month and go home, grumbling and well fed.

choices.text: Tell them what lives in the mine

effects.log: You tell them. They go up to look, come down very quiet, and leave the province.

events.text: On the mountain there is a monk's grave, and beside it a rusted mound shaped like a lying beast. Children leave nails on the mound for luck. Today you climb up with a nail in your fist.

choices.text: Leave the nail

effects.log: You leave it. On the way down you find a coin in the path. You decide it is the mound's thanks.

choices.text: Pull a weed from the monk's grave first

effects.log: You weed the monk's grave before you leave the nail. The rusted mound, you could swear, settles a little, like something sighing.

events.text: The rusted mound beside the monk's grave has a crack in it. A child says it is breathing. You go to see.

choices.text: Leave rice on it

effects.log: You leave rice. The crack closes over by spring, and the children's nails are rusted in all along it like a row of stitches.

choices.text: Sit with it a while

effects.log: You sit. It does not breathe. It never ate again. But it is not lonely, you think, here.

events.text: In the old capital people show visitors a side gate in the north wall that is always left open. A kingdom went out by it, they say, and a beast with it.

choices.text: Walk out through it

effects.log: You walk out through the side gate and along the old road until dark. You do not know why it makes you sad.

choices.text: Ask an old gatekeeper about it

effects.log: "It followed the last king out," the gatekeeper says. "And when the kingdom ended, so did it. Loyal. People forget that part."

events.text: At the old gate, in a crack in the stone, you find a needle as long as your arm, rusted, very old.

choices.text: Leave it where it is

effects.log: You leave it. Some things should stay at the door they went out by.

choices.text: Take it to the old king's tomb

effects.log: You lay it at the old king's tomb. It seems right. The tomb-keeper nods as if he had been expecting it.

events.text: On a winter road in the far north you find footprints in fresh snow, round, each one the size of a cart wheel, going away north past where the maps end.

choices.text: Follow them a day

effects.log: You follow them a day. They go on and on. At dusk you turn back. Some say it still lives. You are now one of them.

choices.text: Leave a broken knife in one

effects.log: You leave an old broken knife in the last print. In the morning the snow has covered everything, except a small round hole where the knife was.

events.text: Traders from beyond the northern border tell of a beast that eats the iron of old battlefields and leaves the grass greener.

choices.text: Ask them which way it went

effects.log: "North," they say. "Always north." You find you are smiling.

choices.text: Buy them a meal for the story

effects.log: You buy them supper. They tell it three ways, all different. You like all three.

events.text: The ferrymen on your river will not drop anchor at the deep pool under the cliffs. If you do, they say, you will haul up a bare rope. On quiet nights, they say, you can hear something chewing down there.

choices.text: Ride the night ferry and listen

effects.log: You ride across at midnight and listen. Very faintly, from under the dark water, comes a slow contented crunching.

choices.text: Drop an old anchor in as an offering

effects.log: You drop an old anchor in. The rope goes slack. The ferryman crosses himself in three religions at once.

events.text: The river floods and the ferry overturns at the deep pool. You go under. Something huge rises underneath and pushes you to the bank.

choices.text: Thank the pool

effects.log: You thank it, soaked, on the bank. Bubbles rise, slowly, like a sigh.

choices.text: Throw in your belt buckle

effects.log: You throw in your iron buckle. It seems the least you can do. Your trousers fall down. The ferrymen are kind enough not to laugh much.

events.text: Clearing out the attic, you find three grains of cooked rice on the floor, still soft, though nobody has eaten up here in years. They are pressed together, almost like four little legs.
events.arc: Three Grains on the Attic Floor

choices.text: Leave them where they are

effects.log: You leave them. In the morning they are gone, and so is the old needle that was stuck in the beam.

choices.text: Set them on a dish, with a needle beside them

effects.log: You set them on a dish with a needle. In the morning the needle is gone and the grains are still there, looking pleased with themselves.

events.text: Small things have gone missing from your house: a pin, a nail, a thimble. Under the floor, at night, a tiny clink, like someone remembering.
events.arc: Three Grains on the Attic Floor

choices.text: Leave out broken things only

effects.log: You leave out broken things only. Nothing whole goes missing again. Whatever it is, it learns fast this time.

choices.text: Say out loud: be good this time

effects.log: You say it. The clinking stops. Then, very quietly, one clink, like a yes.

events.text: There are no swords in the world. There have not been for longer than anyone remembers. Your sect trains with poles and fists, and on the hills lies a dark shape everyone is afraid of.

choices.text: Train harder with the pole

effects.log: You train until your palms are horn. You will never hold a sword. You will be very good with a pole.

choices.text: Ask the elders why everyone fears the hill

effects.log: "It took every sword by force," the elders say. "So nobody fears a sword. Everybody fears it."

events.text: A child in your sect finds a sword in an old grave: the first steel anyone has seen. Everybody looks at the hill.

choices.text: Bury it again, quickly

effects.log: You bury it again, fast, and say nothing. The hill does not stir.

choices.text: Carry it to the hill and offer it, freely

effects.log: You carry it to the hill and hold it out. The dark shape is still a long time. Then a trunk comes down and takes it, very gently. The whole sect saw. It is the first gift it was ever given.

events.text: There is a field where nothing grows in a long trench, and old iron lies rusted across it: needles, spoons, blades, nobody's. The court burned a beast there once, they say, and nobody came to take the iron home.

choices.text: Take one spoon home to someone

effects.log: You take one spoon to the poorest house in the village. It is the first thing that ever went home from that field.

choices.text: Walk the length of the trench

effects.log: You walk it end to end. It takes a long time. At the far end you sit down, and for no reason you can explain, weep.

events.text: You begin, one by one, to carry the iron from the burnt field to the villages it came from, by the marks on it.

choices.text: Keep at it for years

effects.log: It takes you years. By the end, the field is bare earth, and the next spring, for the first time, grass grows in the trench.

choices.text: Get the children to help

effects.log: You turn it into a game. The children carry iron home like treasure. In two summers the field is clear.

events.text: Far off there is a field of rust, and in it lies something huge, dark and still. The proverb says: Songdo's last-days Iron-Eater, which ate until there was no iron left and lay down. You walk to the edge of it.

choices.text: Look at its tail

effects.log: You look at the tail. It is iron, like the rest. You had hoped, you realise, for a single grain of rice.

choices.text: Leave a bowl of rice at its head

effects.log: You leave a bowl of rice at its head. It does not move. You did not expect it to. You leave it anyway.

events.text: Every year the bowl of rice you leave at the rusted beast is untouched. This year, the rice is gone.

choices.text: Leave another

effects.log: You leave another. You will leave one every year as long as you live. Something in you says it is not too late.

choices.text: Say the proverb, but change the end

effects.log: You say the proverb, but end it: "and then it remembered." Nobody else hears. You feel better.
